title: Carotid artery stenosis
seen_note: 436F — exactly like previous OSCEs; 438A — same as previous files
scenario: A 65-year-old hypertensive man (on treatment) with sudden right-sided upper-limb weakness that resolved within minutes. Exam normal apart from a left carotid bruit; brain CT unremarkable. 437A · Archive

imgs.cap: 3D CT angiogram — left internal carotid artery stenosis

qs.q: List 4 risk factors for carotid artery stenosis.
a: Hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, smoking (+ age, male, family history).
qs.why: Carotid stenosis is atherosclerosis — the same risk factors as coronary and peripheral disease.

qs.q: List 3 clinical presentations of carotid stenosis.
a: TIA, ipsilateral transient visual loss (amaurosis fugax), stroke (and asymptomatic bruit).
qs.why: Plaque at the carotid bifurcation throws emboli to the brain (TIA, stroke) or retina via the ophthalmic artery (amaurosis fugax); some are found only as a bruit.

qs.q: What is your next step in investigating this possible carotid stenosis?
a: Carotid duplex ultrasound; CTA or MRA.
qs.why: Duplex ultrasound is non-invasive and grades the stenosis; CTA/MRA confirm it and plan surgery.

qs.q: On the 3D CT picture provided, what is your diagnosis?
a: Left internal carotid artery stenosis.
qs.why: A narrowing at the origin of the left ICA explains a right-sided (contralateral) TIA.

qs.q: What is the best way to manage this patient?
a: Risk-factor modification + medical therapy (antiplatelet/aspirin, statin, ACE-I) + carotid endarterectomy.
qs.why: A symptomatic stenosis (≥ 50–70%) benefits from endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the TIA, plus best medical therapy to stabilise plaque.

qs.q: List 4 complications of the procedure.
a: Stroke, myocardial infarction, bleeding/neck haematoma, cranial-nerve injury (hypoglossal, vagus/recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular branch of facial, glossopharyngeal).
qs.why: Clamping and plaque manipulation can cause stroke; these are arteriopaths at cardiac risk; the neck dissection risks bleeding and the nearby cranial nerves.

tips.t: Dr Al-Jabri: symptomatic with significant stenosis (> 50 %) → surgery. Asymptomatic → usually medical treatment; operate once symptomatic.

title: Varicose veins / chronic venous insufficiency
scenario: A case about an old lady who works as a teacher (prolonged standing). 438F · 442A · Archive

imgs.cap: Leg with varicosities and skin changes (same image as the 442A exam)

qs.q: Take a history.
a: Symptoms: visible veins, aching/heaviness, itching, swelling (worse at the end of the day/standing), night cramps, skin changes, ulcers, bleeding.
Risk factors: prolonged standing (occupation), pregnancy, obesity, family history, previous DVT/leg trauma (secondary), OCP.
qs.why: Ask about the symptoms of venous hypertension (aching, swelling worse on standing), complications (skin changes, ulcers, bleeding) and causes (standing occupation, pregnancy, previous DVT).
hist: The main presenting complaint and cosmetic concern.
Swelling worse at end of day or on standing
Gravity increases venous pressure — typical of venous disease.
Complications that define advanced disease (CEAP class) and are indications for treatment.
Raise venous pressure in the legs.
Strong genetic tendency to valve weakness.
Secondary varicose veins from post-thrombotic damage — changes management.
Hormonal effect on vein walls and clotting.

qs.q: What is your diagnosis?
a: Chronic venous insufficiency (varicose veins).
qs.why: Dilated tortuous superficial veins with symptoms of venous hypertension = chronic venous insufficiency/varicose veins.

qs.q: What is the pathophysiology?
a: Incompetent valves → venous reflux and stasis → venous hypertension.
qs.why: Failed valves let blood reflux down the leg with gravity, raising venous pressure in the superficial veins — they dilate, and skin changes follow.

qs.q: What are the two aetiological causes, and how do you differentiate them?
a: Primary: incompetent superficial valves with a normal deep system.
Secondary: deep-system pathology (previous DVT, AV malformation, pelvic mass compressing the IVC).
Differentiate by history and duplex (± venogram).
qs.why: Primary varicose veins are a superficial valve problem; secondary ones follow deep-vein damage (post-thrombotic) or obstruction — this matters because treating the superficial veins is unsafe if the deep system is blocked.

qs.q: Name the affected vein.
a: Great (long) saphenous vein.
qs.why: The great saphenous vein (medial leg and thigh, to the saphenofemoral junction) is the commonest affected.

qs.q: Investigations that are diagnostic and guide therapy?
a: Duplex ultrasound (non-invasive, diagnostic + guides therapy — 442A wanted ONE); venogram.
qs.why: Duplex shows reflux, its site (SFJ/SPJ) and the patency of the deep veins — it both diagnoses and plans treatment.

qs.q: How do you manage this case?
a: Lifestyle (leg elevation, weight loss, exercise) + compression stockings.
Minimally invasive: radiofrequency ablation (442A answer), endovenous laser, sclerotherapy.
Surgery: high ligation of the sapheno-femoral junction ± stripping.
qs.why: Compression and lifestyle control symptoms; endovenous ablation is first-line for truncal reflux (less pain, faster recovery than surgery); ligation/stripping when ablation isn't suitable.

qs.q: What are the complications?
a: Superficial thrombophlebitis, bleeding (rupture), oedema, skin
pigmentation/lipodermatosclerosis, venous ulcers, infection, DVT & PE.
qs.why: Chronic venous hypertension damages skin (pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, ulcers); dilated veins can thrombose or bleed.

qs.q: How many saphenous veins are there?
a: Two — great (long) and small (short) saphenous veins.
qs.why: The great (long) saphenous drains the medial leg into the femoral vein; the small (short) saphenous drains the back of the calf into the popliteal vein.

qs.q: What do patients complain of?
a: Disfigurement (prominent veins), pain, soreness, cramping, heaviness.
qs.why: Most complain of the appearance and of aching/heaviness from venous congestion.

title: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (rest pain)
scenario: A 55-year-old diabetic, hypertensive smoker (20 years) presents to the ED with rest pain in the calf and absent pulses. Old exam
A patient with rest pain and a history of HTN, DM and smoking; angiogram shown. 439A · 442B
Arteriogram picture + scenario of critical limb ischaemia. 441F

imgs.cap: Angiogram — superficial femoral artery stenosis/occlusion (439A; 442B had a similar picture with popliteal stenosis) Angiogram — femoral artery disease
Angiogram similar to the old-exam picture

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Chronic (critical) limb-threatening ischaemia.
qs.why: Rest pain with absent pulses in a smoker with diabetes = critical (chronic limb-threatening) ischaemia — the limb is at risk.

qs.q: What do such patients present with? / What are the symptoms?
a: Intermittent claudication → rest pain → tissue loss (ulcers, gangrene); absent pulses.
qs.why: Chronic ischaemia progresses from pain on exercise (claudication) to pain at rest (worse at night, relieved by hanging the leg down) to tissue loss.

qs.q: What is the investigation in this image?
a: (Digital subtraction) angiography.
qs.why: Contrast in the arteries with the background subtracted = digital subtraction angiography.

qs.q: Describe what you see. / Which artery?
a: Stenosis/occlusion of the superficial femoral artery (442B: popliteal) with collaterals.
qs.why: Describe the level and type of lesion: a stenosis/occlusion of the SFA (commonest site, adductor canal) with collaterals bypassing it.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, LFT, type & cross-match.
Imaging: Doppler with ABI, duplex, CT angiography, angiogram.
qs.why: Bloods prepare for intervention (renal function for contrast, clotting); ABI/duplex measure severity and CTA/angiography plan revascularisation.

qs.q: What other investigation would you order?
a: Ankle–brachial index (ABI).
qs.why: ABI is simple, bedside and quantifies the severity of arterial disease.

qs.q: What is the normal ABI?
a: 0.9–1.3 (claudication ~0.5–0.9; rest pain < 0.4).
qs.why: Ankle pressure is normally equal to or slightly above arm pressure; lower ratios grade ischaemia, and > 1.3 means calcified incompressible vessels (diabetics).

qs.q: What are the risk factors for atherosclerosis?
a: Modifiable: smoking, DM, HTN, dyslipidaemia, obesity. Non-modifiable: age, male, family history.
qs.why: Atherosclerosis risk factors are divided into those we can change (targets of treatment) and those we can't.

qs.q: How would you manage this patient?
a: Conservative: risk-factor modification (stop smoking), supervised exercise, foot care.
Medical: antiplatelet (aspirin/clopidogrel), statin, ACE-I; analgesia.
Revascularisation: endovascular (angioplasty ± stent) or surgical bypass.
qs.why: Everyone gets risk-factor control and best medical therapy; rest pain means a threatened limb, so revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) is needed to save it.

qs.q: What are the complications of the imaging study shown (angiography)?
a: Local: haemorrhage/haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, dissection, thrombosis/distal embolism, infection.
Systemic: contrast nephropathy/renal failure, anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, heart failure, stroke.
qs.why: Angiography is arterial puncture plus iodinated contrast: local puncture complications and systemic contrast reactions/nephropathy.

qs.q: What medical treatment will you give this patient?
a: Antiplatelet (aspirin; clopidogrel if allergic/PUD), statin (even with normal lipids — anti- inflammatory, slows progression), ACE inhibitor — lifelong.
qs.why: Antiplatelets prevent thrombosis, statins stabilise plaque and lower cardiovascular events, ACE-I protect the vessels — lifelong secondary prevention.

title: Intermittent claudication — aorto-iliac disease (Leriche)
scenario: A 50-year-old man with bilateral buttock/thigh pain on walking 200 m, relieved by rest; absent femoral pulses bilaterally (written station). 430A · 430F
Same scenario in the archive file. Archive

imgs.cap: Angiogram similar to the 430 exam picture (in the exam the Angiogram — aorto-iliac stenosis (arrow) stenosis was bilateral in the external iliac arteries)

qs.q: Mention 4 modifiable risk factors.
a: DM, HTN, hyperlipidaemia, smoking.
qs.why: These four are the modifiable targets — stopping smoking is the most important.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Intermittent claudication (chronic limb ischaemia — aorto-iliac disease).
qs.why: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest = intermittent claudication; buttock/thigh pain with absent femoral pulses places the disease in the aorto-iliac segment.

qs.q: What is the syndrome if associated with impotence?
a: Leriche syndrome (buttock claudication + impotence + absent femoral pulses).
qs.why: Aorto-iliac occlusion reduces flow to the internal iliacs (buttocks, penis) — buttock claudication, impotence and absent femoral pulses = Leriche syndrome.

qs.q: What is the ABI, and what is the normal value?
a: Ratio of ankle to brachial systolic pressure; normal 1.0–1.2 (≈ 0.9–1.3).
qs.why: ABI compares ankle with brachial systolic pressure; < 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease.

qs.q: What type of investigation is this?
a: Angiogram.
qs.why: Contrast-filled arteries on X-ray = angiogram.

qs.q: What abnormality do you see?
a: Bilateral stenosis of the external iliac arteries (Dr Majdi's answer).
qs.why: Identify the vessels and the narrowing — bilateral iliac stenosis explains bilateral buttock/thigh claudication.

qs.q: Mention 4 local complications of this investigation.
a: Pseudoaneurysm, bleeding/haematoma, infection, arterial thrombosis, AV fistula, distal embolisation.
qs.why: Complications at the puncture site come from the hole in the artery (bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula), clot (thrombosis, emboli) and infection.

qs.q: What is the best treatment in this case?
a: Risk-factor modification + medical (antiplatelet, statin, ACE-I) + exercise; revascularisation: angioplasty ± stenting, if failed → surgical bypass.
qs.why: Claudication is treated first with risk-factor control, medicines and exercise; short iliac lesions do very well with angioplasty/stenting if symptoms limit life.

title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
scenario: A 55-year-old with abdominal pain radiating to the back; CT abdomen shown. 439F

imgs.cap: 3D CT angiogram — infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm 3D CT — infrarenal AAA (439F)

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Abdominal (infrarenal) aortic aneurysm.
qs.why: A focal dilatation of the infrarenal aorta ≥ 3 cm is an AAA.

qs.q: What is the most common presentation?
a: Incidental finding (asymptomatic).
qs.why: Most AAAs are silent until found on imaging or screening — or until they rupture.

qs.q: Mention 4 risk factors.
a: Smoking, HTN, hyperlipidaemia, family history, male, old age, race (white).
qs.why: Smoking is the strongest risk factor; male sex, age, family history and hypertension follow.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgery?
a: Ruptured, symptomatic (tender/painful), rapid growth (≥ 1 cm/year; normal ~0.5 cm/year), diameter > 5.5 cm.
qs.why: Rupture risk climbs steeply above 5.5 cm or with rapid growth or symptoms — above this the risk of rupture exceeds the risk of repair.

qs.q: CT shows a 4.5 cm aneurysm — what will you do?
a: Observation with regular US surveillance (+ risk-factor control) — Dr Kaisor: this is the complete answer.
qs.why: Below 5.5 cm the rupture risk is lower than the operative risk, so the aneurysm is watched with serial ultrasound and risk factors controlled.

tips.t: DM is NOT a risk factor (protective) — the doctor asked about it.

title: Acute limb ischaemia
scenario: A patient with DM and atrial fibrillation on warfarin stopped it for a dental procedure, then came with left leg pain and coldness. 435 · Archive

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Acute limb ischaemia.
qs.why: Sudden pain and coldness of a limb = acute limb ischaemia.

qs.q: What is the most common presentation?
a: 6 P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia (perishing cold).
qs.why: The 6 P's are the clinical features of sudden loss of arterial supply; paraesthesia and paralysis mean a threatened limb.

qs.q: What is the cause?
a: Embolism from the heart (AF, warfarin stopped).
qs.why: AF without anticoagulation lets clot form in the left atrium; it embolises to the leg — the commonest cause of acute limb ischaemia.

qs.q: What is your management?
a: ABC; immediate IV heparin (not warfarin — takes ~3 days); urgent revascularisation — embolectomy (Fogarty) / thrombectomy.
qs.why: Heparin immediately stops clot propagation; the embolus must be removed urgently (Fogarty embolectomy) before muscle and nerve die.

qs.q: What are the possible complications of this procedure?
a: Reperfusion syndrome (hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria/rhabdomyolysis), compartment syndrome, recurrent embolisation.
qs.why: Restoring flow to ischaemic muscle releases potassium, acid and myoglobin (reperfusion syndrome) and causes swelling within fascial compartments (compartment syndrome).

qs.q: Examine the diabetic foot / describe the ulcer in detail.
a: Site, size, shape, edge (sloping, punched-out, undermined, rolled, everted), floor/base (granulation, slough, exposed tendon/bone), depth, discharge, surrounding skin, tenderness. Pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal, femoral), capillary refill, temperature; sensation (10 g monofilament, vibration), reflexes; deformities (Charcot, claw toes), regional lymph nodes.
qs.why: Ulcer description (site, edge, floor, base) suggests its cause; the vascular and neurological examination (pulses, monofilament, vibration) identifies ischaemia and neuropathy — the two roots of diabetic foot disease.

qs.q: What are the causes of the ulcer?
a: Ischaemia, neuropathy, infection (+ venous, pressure/trauma).
qs.why: Diabetic ulcers come from neuropathy (unfelt pressure/trauma), ischaemia (poor healing) and infection, often all three.

title: Chronic mesenteric (bowel) ischaemia
scenario: An image to interpret; then risk factors and management (medical & surgical). 439B

imgs.cap: CT/MR angiogram of the coeliac axis, SMA and IMA

qs.q: Interpret the image.
a: Sagittal angiogram showing stenosis/occlusion at the origin of the coeliac axis and/or SMA (mesenteric arteries).
qs.why: A lateral (sagittal) view shows the origins of the coeliac trunk and SMA from the aorta — narrowed at their origins by atherosclerosis.

qs.q: What are the risk factors?
a: Atherosclerosis risk factors: smoking, HTN, DM, dyslipidaemia, age; (AF/embolic source for acute ischaemia).
qs.why: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is atherosclerotic; embolic sources (AF) cause the acute form.

qs.q: What is the management (medical & surgical)?
a: Medical: stop smoking, antiplatelet, statin, nutritional support.
Revascularisation: endovascular angioplasty/stenting (first line) or surgical
bypass/endarterectomy.
qs.why: Patients are malnourished from fear of eating; revascularisation (stenting first, bypass if not possible) relieves the "intestinal angina" and prevents infarction.

qs.q: What are the types and causes of lymphoedema?
a: Primary (congenital, praecox, tarda) vs secondary — axillary/inguinal node dissection, radiotherapy, filariasis, malignancy.
qs.why: Lymphoedema is failure of lymph drainage: primary forms are developmental; secondary forms follow damage to the nodes or lymphatics (surgery, radiotherapy, tumour, filariasis).

qs.q: What are the clinical features?
a: Swelling starting distally, pitting early and non-pitting late; Stemmer's sign — you can't pinch the dorsal skin of the 2nd toe; skin thickening.
qs.why: Protein-rich fluid causes fibrosis of the subcutaneous tissue, so the swelling becomes non-pitting and the skin thickens — Stemmer's sign is specific.

qs.q: What investigations?
a: Lymphoscintigraphy (confirms poor lymphatic drainage); duplex US to exclude DVT.
qs.why: Lymphoscintigraphy shows delayed tracer transport; duplex excludes a venous cause of a swollen limb.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Complex decongestive therapy: manual lymphatic drainage, compression bandaging/garments, skin care, exercise. Surgery for selected cases: lymphovenous anastomosis, lymph-node transfer, debulking.
qs.why: There is no cure — decongestive therapy moves fluid and compression keeps it out; skin care prevents cellulitis, which worsens lymphatic damage. Microsurgery helps selected patients.
